clinicalPearls: Compression of the neurovascular structures traversing the thoracic outlet, classified into neurogenic, venous, and arterial subtypes according to the structure involved
Neurogenic disease is by far the commonest, causing arm and hand pain, paraesthesiae, and weakness, often with wasting of the thenar or intrinsic hand muscles in advanced true neurogenic cases

Venous disease (Paget-Schroetter or effort thrombosis) presents with acute arm swelling, cyanosis, and distended superficial veins, typically after vigorous or repetitive arm use in young active people
Arterial disease is the rarest but most dangerous, causing hand ischaemia, digital emboli, or a subclavian aneurysm, and is strongly associated with a cervical rib or bony anomaly
Predisposing factors include a cervical rib, anomalous first rib, fibrous bands, and hypertrophied scalene muscles, often with a history of repetitive overhead activity or trauma
Provocative manoeuvres and posture-dependent symptoms aid clinical assessment, but imaging and nerve studies are needed to confirm the subtype

Management ranges from physiotherapy and postural correction in neurogenic disease to anticoagulation with venous decompression in effort thrombosis and prompt surgical decompression and arterial repair in the arterial form
reference.pathophysiology: Thoracic outlet syndrome arises from compression of the brachial plexus, subclavian vein, or subclavian artery as they pass through the confined space bounded by the scalene muscles, the first rib, and the clavicle. Congenital factors such as a cervical rib, an anomalous first rib, or fibrous bands narrow this space, while acquired factors including scalene muscle hypertrophy, poor posture, and post-traumatic scarring can further reduce it. Neurogenic compression of the lower brachial plexus produces sensory and motor symptoms in the arm and hand. Venous compression, aggravated by repetitive arm effort, promotes turbulence, intimal injury, and thrombosis of the subclavian vein, the basis of Paget-Schroetter effort thrombosis. Arterial compression, usually against a bony anomaly, damages the subclavian artery wall and can lead to post-stenotic aneurysm, mural thrombus, and distal embolisation causing hand ischaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome and other peripheral entrapment neuropathies
Rotator cuff disease or other shoulder pathology
Raynaud phenomenon or other cause of digital ischaemia
Upper limb deep vein thrombosis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound with positional manoeuvres to assess subclavian vessel compression or thrombosis
CT or MR angiography and venography to define vascular anatomy and bony anomalies
Chest and cervical spine radiographs to identify a cervical rib or first-rib anomaly
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise neurogenic involvement
Catheter venography or arteriography in venous and arterial subtypes, particularly before intervention
MRI of the brachial plexus and thoracic outlet in diagnostically difficult neurogenic cases
redFlags: Hand or digital ischaemia, or a subclavian aneurysm, indicating arterial thoracic outlet syndrome
Acute painful arm swelling and cyanosis suggesting subclavian vein thrombosis
Progressive muscle wasting and weakness in true neurogenic disease
Distal embolic events threatening the hand or fingers
reference.prognosis: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome often improves with conservative physiotherapy and postural measures, with surgery reserved for refractory or true neurogenic cases. Venous effort thrombosis generally does well with anticoagulation and decompression, while arterial disease requires prompt surgical treatment and, once complicated by embolisation or aneurysm, carries the greatest risk to the limb.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing neurogenic disease without objective imaging or neurophysiological support
Missing arterial thoracic outlet syndrome as a source of unexplained hand or digital ischaemia
Failing to identify a cervical rib or bony anomaly driving vascular compression
Treating effort thrombosis with anticoagulation alone without considering decompression
Confusing the syndrome with cervical radiculopathy or distal nerve entrapment
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Confirm the subtype with imaging and nerve studies first, since neurogenic, venous and arterial disease need different treatment

Treat the neurogenic subtype initially with physiotherapy, postural correction and activity modification, reserving surgical decompression by scalenectomy and first-rib or cervical-rib resection for refractory or true neurogenic cases
Manage venous effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) with anticoagulation and catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by thoracic outlet decompression
Treat the arterial subtype with resection of the bony anomaly and repair or reconstruction of the subclavian artery, with thromboembolectomy for distal emboli
Provide analgesia and neuropathic pain control for neurogenic symptoms
Escalate arterial disease urgently given the risk of hand ischaemia, digital embolism and limb loss
Manage within a multidisciplinary team of vascular medicine, vascular or thoracic surgery and neurology
